title: Soupe à l'Oignon
subtitle: French onion soup with Gruyère croutons
excerpt: French onion soup is one of the great dishes of Parisian cooking: deeply caramelised onions in a rich beef broth, topped with bread toasted in the oven and melted Gruyère. The onions must cook for at least 45 minutes -- their caramelisation is the entire flavour base of the soup. Rushing the onions produces a pale, sweet soup with none of the depth of the original.
sourceNotes: Soupe à l'oignon gratinée is a Parisian classic. The dish has been made in Paris since at least the 18th century and was associated with the Les Halles market, where traders and workers ate it in the early hours of the morning. The gratinée (broiled cheese topping) became the defining version in the 19th century. The dish is now one of the most internationally recognised French recipes.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The onion soup base can be made up to 3 days ahead. Add the bread and cheese just before serving.

content.text: The onions take 45 to 50 minutes. They start pale and sharp, then soften, then begin to colour, then slowly turn golden and deeply caramelised. Do not rush this by increasing the heat -- you will burn the edges before the centres soften. Low-to-medium heat and patience is the only technique required.

Melt {{unsalted-butter}} butter with {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} oil in a large, wide pot over medium-low heat. Add {{onion}} onions and {{salt-table}} salt. Cook, stirring every 5 minutes, for 45 to 50 minutes until deep golden and caramelised. If they colour too fast, reduce the heat further.

Add {{garlic}} garlic and {{plain-flour}} flour. Stir for 1 minute. Pour in {{white-wine-dry}} wine and let it bubble for 2 minutes. Add {{beef-stock}} stock, {{thyme-fresh}} thyme, and {{bay-leaves}} bay leaves. Simmer for 20 minutes. Taste for {{salt-table}} salt and {{black-pepper}} pepper.

Preheat the grill to high. Ladle the soup into ovenproof bowls. Float {{bread-white}} toasted bread on top. Pile {{gruyere}} Gruyère over the bread. Grill for 3 to 4 minutes until the cheese is melted and bubbling and beginning to brown. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: The onions have coloured unevenly -- some dark brown, some still pale
items.cause: The heat was too high, or the pan was not large enough for the onion volume.
items.fix: Stir more frequently on high spots. Reduce the heat and add a tablespoon of water to deglaze any dark spots on the pan base. The onions will eventually even out.

content.text: Soupe à l'oignon is the great soup of Paris. It is one of the dishes most associated with the old market quarter around Les Halles, where for two centuries it was served to market workers, night revellers, and travellers arriving on early trains. The cheese gratin topping appeared in the 19th century and became the standard version. The dish is now on the menu of French restaurants around the world.
